newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity called to open steady to lower.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity called to open steady to lower.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were called to open steady to lower Tuesday in line with over-the-counter (OTC) activity after Monday's expiration of the August contracts.

September OTC Palo Verde (PV) were quoted at $30.40-30.75 a megawatt hour (MWh) against Monday's settlement at $30.68, and September OTC California-Oregon Border (COB) was talked at $22.50-22.80 against yesterday's close at $22.95.
August OTC fell about a dollar to $37.00-37.35 and August OTC COB held steady from Monday's settle at $20.25-20.60.
Day-ahead firm, peak deliveries at PV slipped to $34.00-36.00 and at COB $17.25-17.75, market sources said.
On Monday, the August PV contract expired up, while August COB went the off board lower amid to shortcovering and stronger western cash power prices.

The 1,221 megawatt (MW) Palo Verde 2 nuclear power unit in Arizona began slowly coasting down to its September refueling outage. The unit was running at 98 percent early Tuesday, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission said in its daily status report.
The 750 MW Four Corners coal-fired unit 5 in New Mexico, which was shut earlier this month to repair its high pressure generator field, was still planned to restart next week.
Damage to a fish ladder at the Bonneville Dam on Columbia River in Oregon could reduce power output at the project by 200 MW for a month or two.

To clear space for future runoffs, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation was scheduled on Sunday to begin releasing extra water and producing more electricity at its Hoover, Davis and Parker hydroelectric projects.
The Hoover hydropower plant in Nevada has a generating capacity of 1,037 MW, Davis in Arizona 240 MW and Parker in California 120 MW.

On Thursday, southbound transfer capability on the AC segment of the Pacific Intertie transmission system will be cut by 150 MW to 3,300 MW between 1000-1300 PDT due to maintenance on a 500 kilovolt section of the lines.
Final approval from the Western Systems Coordinating Council (WSCC) to increase the intertie's capacity to 6,900 megawatt (MW) from 6,300 is expected later this week.

The latest six to 10 day forecasts showed the West would experience seasonal to slightly cooler-than-seasonal readings regionwide with a monsoonal flow bringing above-normal precipitation in the mountainous areas.
